## XII.

It is therefore established that the fanatic opinions of the <term>Paracelsists</term>, <term>Weigelians</term>, <term>Mystics</term>, <term>Quakers</term>, and others—who are commonly called by the name of the illuminated—concur in this: that besides the body and the rational soul, there is in man a certain substantial part granted to him divinely and, as most do not hide, from the very essence of God. The same doctrine regarding the three parts of man is explained quite prolixly by <term>Felgenhawer</term> in his *Forecourt, in the Holy and Holiest of Holies at the Temple of God* <note>original: "Vorhoff/ im heiligen und Allerheiligsten am Tempel GOttes"</note>; the individual readings of this fanatic booklet sufficiently declare the rationales for the individual parts and the dreams of the fanatics concerning them. It is also worth comparing <term>Bartholomaeus Sclei</term>'s *Decent General Teaching of God* <note>original: "anständige allgemeine GOttes Lehre"</note>, as well as the *Book of the Testimony of the Hidden Field-Treasure* <note>original: "Buch des Zeugnisses des verborgenen Ackerschatzes"</note>, whose author calls himself <term>HIEL</term>, the *One-Essence Life of God* <note>original: "einwesige Leben GOttes"</note>, as well as the *Thorough Instruction* <note>original: "gründlicher Unterricht"</note> of <term>Matthes Weyer</term>, who was highly enlightened by God, and similar portents of books composed by those furies, truly unworthy of anyone wasting good and irrevocable hours reading them.

## XIII.

Moreover, this doctrine concerning the triple part of man occupies a primary place in their own <term>Matæologia</term> <gloss>vain or empty talk/foolish science</gloss>. For the author of the *Forecourt* claims, most ineptly, in Chapter XII that this contains the foundation not only of all Christianity but of all wisdom in general that is in heaven and on earth. But indeed, if by chance it were hidden from someone that he possesses five senses, or what the nature of sight or hearing or the rest might be, must it therefore be established that they are unable to perform their duty? I, for one, do not think so. Meanwhile, <term>Andreas Christoph Rafelius</term> extols this dogma with such great praises that he does not fear to speak of it in this manner in *The New Year's Trumpet* <note>original: "Der Neujahrs Posaune"</note>: "This is actually the right foundation stone and the certain foundation upon which the house of our Christianity shall be set, laid, and founded, if it is to stand: and from this everything—preaching, reading, writing, hearing the Word of God, singing, praying, good"

<summary>The author critiques the "fanatical" belief in a third divine substance in man, citing various works by figures such as Felgenhawer and Matthes Weyer, and argues that this belief is incorrectly elevated by proponents to the central foundation of all Christianity.</summary>
<keywords>Paracelsians, Weigelians, Mystics, Quakers, Felgenhawer, Bartholomaeus Sclei, HIEL, Matthes Weyer, Andreas Christoph Rafelius, three parts of man, fanaticism, Matæologia</keywords>

# On Natural Questions.

<meta>continues from previous page: they had been sent.</meta> They said they had traveled a long journey, having been provided with assistance by the king of Ethiopia and having reached the furthest regions through the recommendations of the kings. We came to immense swamps, they said, whose end even the inhabitants did not know, and which no one can hope to traverse. The reeds and water are so tangled together that they are not navigable except by a small boat capable of carrying only one person, and even that is barely supported by the muddy and overgrown swamp. There, they said, we saw two rocks from which a massive force of river water poured out. Whether that is the source of the <term>Nilus</term> <gloss>the Nile river</gloss>, or whether it is merely an addition, or whether it is born there or returns to the earth after having finished its previous course, is unknown. Do you not believe that it, whatever it is, rises from a great subterranean lake? For it must have moisture scattered in many places, and collected in the depths so that it can erupt with such force. 

Some judge that earthquakes are caused by fire, though they do not all agree on the same cause. Primarily <term>Anaxagoras</term> <gloss>a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher</gloss>, who thinks the earth is shaken by almost the same cause as the air. When, in the lower parts, a spirit <note>referring to breath or wind</note> pushes the dense air and collects it into clouds, it ruptures them in the same way that clouds are accustomed to breaking among us. From this collision of clouds, the fire of lightning flashes out. The spirit itself rushes into what is in its way, seeking an exit, and tears apart the resisting earth until it finds a path to the sky through narrow openings, or creates one by force or by violence. Others judge that fire is indeed a cause, but not for this reason. They argue that it burns in many places it encounters and consumes everything nearby. If these burned-out areas ever collapse, the motion follows in those parts that, deprived of the supports beneath them, wobble until they fall, with nothing occurring to catch the weight. Then it is calmed. Then vast chasms <unclear>remain</unclear>

## On Lettuce. Chapter XXII.

Lettuce, as Isidorus says, is named from the abundance of its milky humor, or because it fills nursing women with milk. In men, it restrains the movement of <term>Venus</term> <gloss>sexual desire</gloss>. Its species is twofold: namely, domestic, and wild, which we call <term>feralia</term> <gloss>wild/brutal</gloss> because its back has hard thorns in the manner of iron, as Isidorus says in book seventeen, the last chapter. Regarding this, Pliny says in his works on diet: wild lettuce is similar in form to the domestic, but it has longer, thinner, rougher, and less green leaves on account of the scarcity of its moisture, and therefore it has much bitterness and astringency with respect to that which is domestic, because it is of greater heat and dryness. Many say that it induces menstruation and expels raw humors, as Dioscorides says. 

Domestic lettuce is cold and moist according to the degree, and in neither quality does it exceed measure, and therefore its use is of grave medicine. It is thin, light, and soft if it is fresh, and therefore it is quickly digested and calms the burning and biting of the stomach and red bile. It refrigerates the boiling of the blood, calms insomnia, and heals headache and choleric fumes. It increases milk in women and generates and augments semen in men; this happens on account of the goodness of the blood that it generates in perfect quantity and at a perfect age. But when it becomes old and hard, its moisture is diminished and it becomes bitter, and through its use the worst blood is generated; the visual power then fails and is weakened, the cause of which is the mortification of the animal sense, because with its astringency it suffocates the natural spirit. Therefore, such lettuce is most harmful to those wishing to generate, for it congeals the material and coagulates the semen, especially if its seed is taken often in food or drink. Isaac says this in his works on diet. 

Pliny, however, in book twenty, chapter eight, says about lettuce: there is a species of lettuce born spontaneously which they call <term>caprina</term> <gloss>goat lettuce</gloss>, which, if cast into the sea, kills the fish that are in the vicinity. Its stalk and leaves, when obtuse, heal incised nerves with applied salt. There is another species of lettuce that grows in fields, whose leaves, when crushed with pearl barley and applied, heal ulcers; the Greeks call this <term>ysopon</term> <gloss>hyssop</gloss>. A third species is that which grows in woods, which they call <term>steraton</term> <gloss>wood-lettuce</gloss>, whose leaves, when crushed with <unclear>purescentia</unclear>, heal wounds; with their root and leaves they mitigate <term>ignis sacer</term> <gloss>the sacred fire/erysipelas</gloss>. There is also another species of this lettuce, round and short, which many call <term>beratia</term> <gloss>likely a variant of hieracia/hawkweed</gloss>, whose juice hawks [use] by scratching...

<column-break/>

...and by tinting their eyes therewith, they dispel obscurity and dimness when they grow old. The juice of this herb heals the ailments of the eyes, and with it, one mixes woman's milk. It heals the bites of serpents and the stings of scorpions if its juice is drunk with wine and its crushed leaves are plastered over the wound. It also dispels and suppresses every swelling. The seed of lettuce, both wild and domestic, suppresses imaginations of lust in dreams and does not allow the body to be polluted if it is taken frequently in food; nevertheless, its frequent and excessive use causes obscurity to the eyes. Pliny attributes many other praises to it in the same chapter, but these suffice.

## On Burdock. Chapter XXIII.

Burdock is an herb having broad and thick leaves around the earth, having at the summits of its stalks certain thorny and aculeated heads, but curved, which are wont to adhere to the garments of those passing by. Hence Isidorus says in book seventeen: burdock is named because it has stalks disposed toward the earth, and it is called by the Greeks <term>philatropos</term> <gloss>man-lover</gloss>, because it adheres to the garments of men on account of its roughness. It is born near walls, and [is called] <term>philatropos</term>, i.e., "loving man," because with a certain affection it seems to adhere to the garments of a man. The species of burdock are twofold: acute and round, disposed to the likeness of a horse's foot, so that by many it is called <term>ungula caballina</term> <gloss>coltsfoot</gloss>, and the leaves of both are of a horrible odor and taste alike, as Dioscorides says. 

But Pliny says in book twenty-six: there are many species of burdock, and all are medicinal. For they heal the stings of scorpions, nor do they strike a man if he has been anointed with its juice. The decoction of its root helps the teeth and also confirms them if held tepid in the mouth. Its seed taken internally cures ailments of the stomach; to those vomiting blood, it is beneficial and assists in cases of dysentery. For its root with wine stops the flow of the bowels, but taken alone, it helps those with stones. The whole herb crushed with lard is valid against scrofula. According to the works of Pliny, as Platearius says, burdock or <term>lappacium</term> <gloss>burdock</gloss> is a hot and dry herb having the power of dissolving, relaxing, opening, and attenuating; and therefore it is valid against scabies, itching, <term>ferpigo</term> <gloss>a skin eruption</gloss>, and impetigo, and it draws humors from the intercutaneous flesh. It dissolves the hardness and tumor of apostemes. It is valid against cold dropsy and the obstruction of the spleen. Its juice mixed with rue purges the brain and rheumatic flow if [used] in a small quantity.

On Lettuce. Chapter XXII.

It has a twofold species: namely, domestic and wild, which we call feral because its back has hard spines like iron, as Isidore says in book XVII, the final chapter. Regarding this, Pliny says in his works on diet: wild lettuce is similar in form to domestic, but it has longer, thinner, rougher, and less green leaves on account of the scarcity of its moisture. And for this reason, it has much bitterness and sharpness in comparison to that which is domestic, because it is of greater heat and dryness. And therefore many say that it provokes menses and expels crude humors, as Dioscorides says. Domestic lettuce is cold and moist according to the degree, and it does not exceed the mean in either quality. It settles the burning and biting of the stomach and red bile; it refrigerates the boiling of blood; it calms insomnia; and it cures headache and choleric fumes. But when it grows old and hardens, its moisture is diminished and it becomes bitter; and by its use, very poor blood is generated. Burdock is a herb having broad and thick leaves around the ground, having at the tops of its stalks certain thorny and prickly little heads that are curved, which are accustomed to adhere to the garments of those passing by. Whence Isidore says in book XVII: Burdock is called so because it has stalks arranged toward the ground, and in Greek it is called *philatropos*, because it adheres to the clothing of men on account of its roughness. It is born near walls, and it is called *philatropos*, that is, "loving man," because with a certain affection it seems to adhere to the clothes of man. There are two species of burdock, pointed and round, arranged in the likeness of a horse's foot, wherefore it is called by many "horse-hoof." The leaves of both are of a horrible odor and taste, as Dioscorides says. But Pliny says in book XXVI: There are many species of burdock, and all are medicinal. ### On the nature of gold

**S**hould one object to these points concerning the nature of gold, which alone, according to <term>Hermes</term> <gloss>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage of alchemy</gloss>, is the metal in which no sickness appears. For neither part of its material is infected or intemperate. Since, like all other metals, it is composed of sulfur and quicksilver, its sulfur is most lucid and clean, and, having been brought to purity through the most powerful washings, it possesses no combustible greasiness at all, nor any watery, phlegmatic humidity capable of evaporation. It has been sublimated and digested in concave places where the solid surface is often <unclear>sublimated and digested by a temperate</unclear> heat, in a digestion process that is called <term>pepasis</term> <gloss>maturation</gloss>. The earthy substance that is incorporated into the sulfur is clean, very subtle, and suspended vaporously throughout the entire substance of the radical moisture of that sulfur. Because of this, it follows that the heat of that sulfur is constitutional, departing in no way from temperament; and this is like the masculine virtue in the composition of gold. Similarly, its quicksilver has two substances cleansed to the extremes. For the third element, which is in the heat itself, is subtilized, not only materially divided, but is most subtle vaporously, having been often sublimated in the cavities of the earth by the life-giving heat of the sun and the stars. Similarly, the watery element is also subtilized in the same manner of repeated subtilization, and since glass is present in this way, it is subtilized finely. It is evident that when mixed together by heat and the disposition of the place that fosters and reflects the vapor upon itself, they are bound together by the most powerful bond of mixture. Sulfur does not enter into the composition of gold merely by quality, but by substance, and since it is a subtle substance, it will penetrate everywhere through the quicksilver, and by coagulating, it colors it. And since both are brought by sublimation to the form of the superior elements, which in the nature of transparency arrive with a perpetual body, each will have full purity. And when many parts of the matter are thickened, they will stand together; this indeed is a property of a subtle substance, that standing together through coagulation, it will have many parts in a very small space. Therefore, the contracted transparency will make a citrine color, and the subtlety makes great solidification, and the constancy of many parts together in a small place and position makes weight, just as is proven from those things which have been reasonably demonstrated in the *Physics* and the *De Caelo*. It follows, however, from the solidification and temperament together that gold is little evaporable or not at all; therefore, it is almost odorless. Although an odor is not essentially a smoky evaporation, a strong odor is nevertheless frequently found with a smoky evaporation, because of which it further follows that gold is more incorruptible than any metal and more resistant to fire because of the strongest commixtion of its mixture. For a smoky evaporation indicates a certain corruption of bodies, which is less in silver and more in copper. PREFACE

Most recently, G. Koertius initiated a study on that part of the *Cynegeticus* <note>On Hunting</note> which is called technical, but he was overtaken by death before he could bring it to completion. He first set forth that not only is the arrangement inconvenient, but the instruction itself is so incomplete and obscure that it could hardly be useful to hunters. It must be admitted that he argued this with justice, but it confirms our conjecture concerning the origin of this little book. For the heir of Xenophon, a man certainly not unversed in rhetorical studies, but little skilled in writing, preserved the series of things just as he had found them written in the volume handed down to him, nor did he dare to add anything from his own knowledge that might clarify the rules or reduce them to a suitable order.

But many of the precepts in this part of the work, Koertius says, are so false that they could by no means have been written by a man truly experienced in hunting. He was prevented by fate from explaining and establishing this opinion with a full number of examples. But at least some of those things which he criticized, or was about to criticize, I would say are controversial rather than false. For the writer of the *Cynegeticus* advises that the hunter should hand the hare over to the hounds to be torn apart once it has been caught by them. Koertius criticizes this advice as plainly absurd. But this very thing is recommended by Blanius, a man no less knowledgeable in the art of hunting than Koertius. What then? In the book *De Re Equestri* <note>On Horsemanship</note>, Xenophon praises Simon for having taught that the quality of the feet in a horse is revealed by the sound; this is what Bourgelatus and Berenger declare to be clearly false. Regarding these and similar matters, learned men fight among themselves, nor would anyone easily judge what is right or true in any given art. Therefore, not

**coinage** <note>original: "νόμισμα"</note> signifies two things: the customary habit, as *Aristophanes* in *Clouds* <gloss>249</gloss> "We have no customary way," and the minting of stamped bronze. The Byzantines used small coinage.

**lawgivers** <note>original: "νομογράφοι"</note> <note>refers to the Decemviri</note>. Among the Romans, in the three-hundred and first year after the founding of the city, the office of the consuls having been abolished, ten lawgivers were entrusted with the protection of public affairs; for a certain time, interpreting laws for the profit and pleasure of the citizens, they seemed moderate and most fit to rule over all. For they recorded the ten tablets with local and Greek laws and set them up on the so-called *kyrbeis* <gloss>three-sided tablets for laws</gloss>. In the second year of their rule, having incurred the charge of tyrannical weight, they were dissolved, especially since *Appius* moved the masses to hatred of the decemvirate, he who plotted to ravish the virgin *Verginia*, the daughter of a man not obscure in military affairs, having become seized with a hot passion for the girl; whom her father killed with his own hand, fearing the power of *Appius* and that he would force the girl to dishonor. Upon this, the entire military was moved and took away the power of the ten, and forced them to pay penalties for the wrongs committed during their tenure.

**legislation** <note>original: "νομοθεσία"</note> the setting of a law.

**lawgivers** <note>original: "νομοθέται"</note> in ancient times *Moses*, and afterward *Christ Jesus*.

The nature of a certain good thing comes from outside. Not even these [should be] as preparing against the enemy, [nor] to be tripped up by the affairs of others or the neighbors, or even by the agreements of the neighbors themselves. Therefore, when it is reported that enemies are preparing against us, it is necessary first to set things in safety, just as was said before, such as the cities and the regions. Then, one must aim for [defensive] desperation, overseeing those things that are changed, [and] the specific places through which they intend to pass, [to see if] it is, for us, an opportunity for an ambush, a clear battle, or [something] advantageous to us. Regarding the things we are carrying, whether we eat [or not], or if we are campaigning with others, the enemies report to us—for [this] brings advantage to us and we [must] be burdened by the wars—and likewise, even if others are campaigning from among them, or if it is a civil war, or a neighbor is remaining quiet, [one must] be a peacemaker regarding most of their own, [while] the enemies look to those from foreign tribes. However, it is necessary for the neighbors to be [as] those who have descended, [so that] each of those who are privy to the mysteries might return his own [things]. Both neighbors must be acting securely toward one another, as one must deliberate for all of them, and [see] if and in what manner [they will act]. Inside the place, only the marketplace—according to which many of our own and the foreign tribes ascend—[must be watched], while looking toward [the interests of] commerce. For in this [location] they will be able to take the enemies more [easily]. Whence, as the day proceeds, [if] again the same [events occur]—the others [providing] their own things, rewarding [us for] the wars, and declaring to us what our enemies are saying and how those of theirs are hostile—[it is clear what to do]. ### CANTO XXI. OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE.

Noble matter, and nobly treated in this twenty-first canto. In which he sets forth how, as they continued their journey, they were rejoined by a soul, from whom they understood the cause of the shaking of the mountain and of the song of the souls. And finally, they recognized that this man had been a poet, and in supreme joy Virgil recognized him.

<column-break/>

<note>A large historiated initial 'L' depicts two figures in a landscape, representing the meeting of Dante and Virgil with the spirit of Statius. The initial is framed in a square border with decorative elements.</note>

The natural thirst that is never sated
except with the water for which the young
Samaritan woman asked for grace,
was tormenting me, and haste was goading me
along the encumbered path behind my guide,
and I was sympathizing with the just vengeance.
And behold, just as Luke describes for us
that Christ appeared to two who were on the way,
already gone forth from the sepulchral cave,
there appeared to us a shade, and behind us it was coming,
looking down at the feet of the crowd that lies,
nor did we notice it until it spoke first,
saying, "My brothers, may God give you peace."
We turned immediately, and Virgil
rendered to it the gesture that is appropriate.

<column-break/>

THE NATURAL THIRST. He shows that there is an innate thirst and desire in man to know. And because the knowledge of divine things is that by which we are blessed, and we cannot have this perfectly through our own industry, nor by a natural path, if we are not illuminated by the Holy Spirit—which Christ signified in the Gospel of Saint John, chapter 4, when asking for a drink from the Samaritan woman at the well of Jacob, and she denied it to him, alleging that the Jews do not associate with the Samaritans—he replied, "If you knew who it is that asks you for a drink, you would ask him, and he would give you a drink of the water of a spring that leaps into eternal life." The young woman, therefore, after many words, asked for it, and Christ filled her with the Holy Spirit. Wherefore, very wisely, the poet here demonstrates that the natural thirst—that is, the natural desire to know and understand—is never sated except with the water for which the young Samaritan woman asked for grace—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit. WAS TORMENTING ME. If a yellow straight vapor appears by the sun, it indicates a ruler establishing his position, while a blue-red straight vapor indicates a subject establishing his own position. 

If the straight vapor in the center is red and the exterior is blue, those who seek to establish their own position will not succeed. If the vapor is yellow and white with a lustrous sheen, they will succeed.

If the blue and red vapors appear like two straight lines intersecting, positioned above, below, or to the sides of the sun, this is called an **Intersecting Embrace** <term>original: *jiaojiao* (交交)</term>; it signifies licentiousness. Vapor of this type suggests the presence of lewd conduct. If there are intersecting red clouds beside the sun, there will be military conflict beneath them.

If two vapors intersect, penetrate, or face back-to-back on both sides of the sun, all these portend major military conflicts for the realm. They also signify internal chaos and discord within the army. It is said that when these intersecting vapors appear beside the sun, the side that strikes from the direction of the intersection will be victorious.

If these vapors form a shape like the character for "mouth" <term>original: *kou* (口)</term> at the edge of the sun, it is called a **Sun-Mouth**. One or two of these "mouths" signify treachery and harm. Three, four, or five "mouths" signify that feudal lords or princes are plotting to seize the throne.

This is what he says. He also says that a wound may occur where it necessitates complete amputation. If the wound has caused much of the member <note>the limb or organ</note> to be cut away, it requires agents that promote the growth of flesh. It is not enough to simply use drying and preventative agents. In fact, the drying and preventative agent might, in some respects, repel the material from which the flesh grows. Sometimes there is a depth and a deficiency in the bone such that it cannot grow back completely, and a cavity remains. A condition may occur where more than necessary grows, resulting in excessive flesh. It is necessary to monitor the patient who requires flesh growth in a wound to ensure it does not grow to an unsightly excess. The growth agent should be such that it allows the flesh to grow. As for the skin, if it has been completely severed, flesh grows in its place that is firm and on which no hair or veins grow. Rather, branches are generated, and it grows like flesh.

Among the wounds, there are dangerous wounds: those occurring in the nerves and the muscles of the upper arm, which we will mention in the chapter on nerves. Often, ominous and severe symptoms follow them. The worst that follows a wound to the upper arm is a change in color and the cessation of the pulse, followed by a trace and shrinking, leading to night-blindness and a failure of strength. Convulsions may also follow it. The same applies to those occurring in front of the knee at the kneecap, for they are followed by severe symptoms, and they are difficult, rarely healing. If a convulsion occurs from such wounds of the upper arm and treatment does not heal it, the treatment is amputation of the upper arm.

For just as natural Magic uses natural causes, so superstitious Magic uses signs that are moral causes; for by these, through a pact, a demon is enticed to do what the Magician requests, and thus the signs themselves appear to accomplish something, as St. Augustine suggests in *City of God*, book 12, chapter 6, where he also teaches that these signs and the entire discipline were first instituted by demons, who nevertheless are not delighted by the signs viewed in themselves, but insofar as they are honored by them, or insofar as they depend on their institution. The organ of sadness is the mouth of the stomach. For this is what feels the gnawing sensation during times of sorrow. As Galen says in the sixth book of his *Demonstrative Treatise*: "In those who are sorrowful, no small amount of yellow bile flows down into the stomach. This causes a gnawing sensation for them, and they do not stop being sorrowful and suffering this gnawing until they have vomited up the bile."

Indeed, the gnawing sensation occurs for them below the cartilage at the center of the chest, which is called the xiphoid <term>xiphoeidēs</term> <gloss>sword-shaped</gloss> process. But the heart is situated much higher up. For in relation to the diaphragm, the stomach is lower, while the heart is higher. The ancients, however, usually call both the heart and the mouth of the stomach by the name of heart, as Hippocrates does, and Thucydides when he speaks of the plague in this way: "And whenever it settled into the heart, it would turn it upside down and cause purgings of bile. All those that had been named by physicians would follow." For that which is turned upside down is the mouth of the stomach being forced to vomit, not the organ of the heart itself.

In the time of the emperor Theophilus, Scholasticius the door-keeper was chamberlain, and in the time of Michael, son of Theophilus, the patrician Damian was chamberlain and after him, in the same reign, Basil, the Christ-loving emperor, was chamberlain. In the time of Basil, the Christ-loving sovereign, there was no chamberlain during all his reign. In the time of Leo, the Christ-loving sovereign, the patrician Samonas was chamberlain, and after him, in the time of the same emperor, the patrician Constantine. In the time of Alexander the emperor, the patrician Barbatus was chamberlain; and in the time of Constantine, the Christ-loving sovereign, the patrician Constantine, mentioned before in the time of the sovereign Leo, was chamberlain again; and in the time of the sovereign Romanus, the patrician Theophanes; and in the second reign of Constantine, the patrician Basil.

In the time of Leo, the Christ-loving and ever-memorable emperor, lived the late Ktenas, an aged cleric of great wealth, who was precentor of the New Church and was skilled in singing as was no other at that time. This same Ktenas besought the patrician Samonas, who was at that time chamberlain, to intercede for him with the emperor so that he might be made <term>protospatharius</term> <gloss>a high court rank</gloss> and wear the shirt and go in procession to the Lausiacus <note>a ceremonial hall in the Great Palace</note> and take his seat as <term>protospatharius</term> and receive a stipend of one pound, and in respect of this remuneration might give the emperor forty pounds. But the emperor could not bring himself to do this, saying that it was out of his power, and <note>original: "τοῦτο..."</note> «to the great disgrace of my imperial majesty if a cleric becomes <term>protospatharius</term>». On hearing this from the patrician Samonas, this same Ktenas added to the forty pounds a pair of ear-rings valued at ten pounds, and a silver table with animals on it in gold relief, also valued at ten pounds. And the emperor, besought by the request of the patrician Samonas, the chamberlain, took the forty pounds of gold and the pair of ear-rings and the table with its gold on silver relief work, so that the total gift of the same Ktenas amounted to sixty pounds. Then the emperor made him <term>protospatharius</term>, and he received a stipend on that occasion of one pound. After being honoured with the rank of <term>protospatharius</term> this same Ktenas lived two years and then died; and he received a stipend of one pound for each of the two years.

For these, it is necessary to adjust them by positioning the lips over a larger or smaller part of the flute's opening, while providing a stronger or weaker wind. This is exactly what a human player does for the same tones, as they are obliged to manage their breath and turn the flute more or less inward or outward.

It is easy to conceive that all the plates placed on the cylinder are of varying lengths, depending on the duration required for each note and the different positions the fingers must occupy to form them. I will not detail this here, for fear of exceeding the limits of a concise memoir, which is all I have proposed to provide.

I will merely remark that, for the swelling of sounds, it was necessary during the duration of a single note to imperceptibly substitute a weak wind for a strong one, and to a stronger wind, a weaker one, while simultaneously varying the movements of the lips—that is to say, placing them in the proper position for each strength of wind.

When it was necessary to perform softly, that is, to imitate an echo, we were obliged to make the lips advance over the edge of the flute's hole and send a wind sufficient to form such a tone; however, its return, through an opening as small as that of its entry into the flute, can only strike a small quantity of external air. This produces, as I mentioned above, what is called an echo.

The different tempos of slowness and speed were measured on the cylinder by means of a lever, one extremity of which was armed with a point that could mark the cylinder when pressed down.

At the other arm of the lever was a spring, which made the point snap back up promptly.

We released the mechanism, which made the cylinder rotate at a speed determined for all the melodies.

At the same time, a person played the melody to be measured on the flute, while another beat time on the end of the lever that marked the cylinder. The distance found between the points was the true measure of the melodies we wished to record; we then subdivided the intervals into as many parts as the measure had beats.

Just as light is the cause of the perception of form, so is an external object the cause of the transformation of the mind. Just as fire is the cause of that which is to be cooked. The knowledge of smoke is the cause of the knowledge of fire. The practice of the limbs of Yoga is the cause of attainment of discriminative knowledge. 

The same is the cause of separation from impurity. The cause of distinctness is, for example, the goldsmith in relation to gold. Thus, in the case of a single perception of a woman, ignorance is the cause of infatuation, and aversion is the cause of the perception of suffering.

<column-break/>

Through all the roots of virtue I have accumulated, may the precious, unsurpassable enlightenment be attained for the benefit of all beings. May all embodied beings in this world possess happiness and the causes of happiness. Having been freed from suffering and the causes of suffering, may they never be separated from supreme bliss itself. Furthermore, the accumulation of merit results in the great wealth of enjoyments, and the accumulation of wisdom results in the wisdom of the sphere of reality <term>dharmadhātu</term> <gloss>the ultimate nature of phenomena</gloss> and so forth. Thus, from the perfection of the two accumulations, the fruit of the two bodies <note>dharmakāya and rūpakāya</note> will arise. There, the truth body <term>dharmakāya</term> is the ultimate body for one's own benefit, and the form body <term>rūpakāya</term> is the relative body for the benefit of others. Thus, the meaning of the two bodies is to possess the unsurpassed intention of benefit and happiness for all beings without exception. Likewise, because all phenomena are pure by nature, the luminosity of one’s own mind is the truth body itself.

And so forth, he continued to grant [teachings] and remain. Then, regarding the upper direction, it is explained that the door of the reversal of emptiness first offered a prayer. From the remaining [teachings], the clarity of the teachings was shown during the period when the three remained in the meadow. Thus it was made clear, and since the entire direction of emptiness was filled with the correct measure, he arrived in the form of an emanation. After the assembly of the three and the entry of the powerful Lord of Destruction <note>an epithet for a wrathful deity or Shiva repurposed in a Buddhist context</note>, he performed the great emptiness and remained. 

Then, on the twelfth day, an auspicious date in the fire-horse year, the work of constructing the monument <note>original: "མཆོད་རྟེན་" (chorten/stupa)</note> was completed through the armor of artistic mastery. Having finished the task of the fine drawings, he met with the senior master of the monastery and remained. 

The Lord himself remained in a state of clear visualization. Through the empowerment of the Noble Lady White Tara <note>original: "སྒྲོལ་དཀར་" (Drolkar)</note>, he did not omit any part of the ritual for the purpose of the empowerment of the <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>the Thus-Gone One; a Buddha</gloss>. Within the assembly of the kingdom, at the very peak of the victorious central government, the Dharma King, the Lord of Loving Kindness <note>Maitreya</note>, found the power of speech. This close companion remained for a long time, turning the wheel of Dharma without interruption. In the presence of the supreme teacher, the Protector Mi-pham <note>The Unconquered Lord, Maitreya</note>, he arrived at that field which is equal to the great Ganden Dharma Gate <note>Ganden is the monastery of Maitreya; the name means Joyous</note> at the crown of the seat of the Lord, and remained clearly shown. 

Then, the Guru of this place, the supreme Chokyi Wangchuk <note>original: "ཆོས་ཀྱི་དབང་ཕྱུག་" (Lord of Dharma)</note>, remained within the assembly of the golden-colored deities.

Through the clarity of these and other points, having attained the measure of the entire direction of emptiness, he arrived in an emanated form. The three gatherings and the powerful lord of destruction entered and performed the great void, and remained. 

Then, on the twelfth day, an auspicious date in the Fire-Horse year <note>1726 or 1786 CE depending on the cycle</note>, he took up the armor of constructing a <term>stupa</term> <gloss>reliquary monument</gloss>. The work was perfectly completed by the skilled artists. Afterward, he met with the senior master of the teachings <note>original: "མཚན་སློབ་བགྲེས་པོ་" (tshen lob drepo)</note> to accomplish the invitation and remained there. 

Regarding his own presence, he clearly visualized the Noble Lady White Tara <note>original: "སྒྲོལ་དཀར་" (Dolkar)</note>. By the power of the initiation of the <term>Tathagatas</term> <gloss>Buddhas; those who have gone thus</gloss>, no part of the ritual was omitted. Amidst the gathering of the kingdom, at the supreme peak of the victorious central government, during that very time, the Heart-Brother of the Lord of Love, the Dharma King <note>Maitreya</note>, who had mastered the power of speech, remained for a long time and turned the wheel of Dharma without interruption. This realm, which is equal to the Great Gate of Dharma at <term>Ganden</term> <gloss>Joyous Mountain; the monastery of Tsongkhapa</gloss> where the Supreme Teacher, the Protector <term>Mipham</term> <gloss>The Unconquered One; Maitreya</gloss> resides, was clearly shown as the place he arrived and stayed. Then, this very lama, the supreme Lord of Dharma, Chokyi Wangchuk, remained with the assembly of deities of the Golden Color.

Remembering his former life, that boy very quickly came to offer a sacrifice of gratitude to the Blessed One. Because the Buddha taught him the Dharma, he attained the fruit of <term>Stream-enterer</term> <gloss>the first stage of enlightenment</gloss>. At that time, a great radiance of light appeared. When the buffalo herders saw this, doubt arose in them. They approached the Blessed One and asked, "Who is it that creates this great radiance of light?" The Buddha then explained how the buffalo had been reborn as a god, which filled the herders with wonder. They thought, "If even one born in the state of an animal can achieve such a result, why should we not also attain something special?" After they had satisfied the Blessed One and the monastic community with fine food, they were ordained. Through great diligence, they directly realized the state of an <term>Arhat</term> <gloss>one who has attained liberation</gloss>.

Once, while the Blessed One was staying in the Jeta Grove, King Prasenajit prepared to pay him honor. The King of Panchala sent five hundred geese as a gift to King Prasenajit of Kosala, and those geese were also offered at the Jeta Grove. Whenever the Buddha and the monastic community sat to take their meals, those geese would go before the Blessed One. The Blessed One and the great disciples gave them scraps of food. After eating, the geese were satisfied, their senses became clear, and they stayed there. Most of them became weary of the world through the Blessed One’s Dharma.

Then, Utpala bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and made this request: "Please teach me the Dharma so that I may be completely liberated from this body of blood and pus through a small amount of merit." As the Blessed One taught the Dharma, some in that assembly attained the fruit of a <term>Stream-enterer</term>. Some attained the fruit of a <term>Once-returner</term> <gloss>the second stage of enlightenment</gloss>. Some attained the fruit of a <term>Non-returner</term> <gloss>the third stage of enlightenment</gloss>. Some attained the state of an <term>Arhat</term>. Utpala also found faith in the Buddha, was ordained, and through great diligence in practice, directly realized the state of an <term>Arhat</term>. The dancers also directly realized the state of an <term>Arhat</term>.

Furthermore, while the Blessed One was staying in the forest called Kachangala, an old woman named Kachangala lived in that region. She took a jar and went to a well for water. The Blessed One said to Ananda, "Go and tell that old woman to offer water for the Blessed One to drink." Ananda went and spoke those words. She replied, "The Noble One himself should come, and I shall offer it."
